newsitem.title: GERMANY: Germany's Kohl draws fire on record jobless rate.
newsitem.headline: Germany's Kohl draws fire on record jobless rate.

text.p: German Chancellor Helmut Kohl drew fire over the weekend as the head of a key labour union blamed his government for Germany's record-high jobless rate, and politicians said he was incapable of solving the problem.
"The record-high unemployment rate is a result of the federal government's policies," Herbert Mai, the head of Germany's public sector service workers OeTV, told German newspaper Express.

Speaking two days after Germany reported its unemployment rate had climbed to 12.2 percent, or 4.66 million, in January from December's 10.8 percent to the highest level since 1933, Mai said the jobless rate could not be halved with current policies.
"We do not create jobs by cutting workers' sickpay or paring back job protection measures," Mai said, adding that "with the current policies, there will be no reducing the unemployment rate by half."
In a bid to save costs, the German government in October passed a highly controversial new law allowing employers to cut workers' pay to 80 percent during illness.

Kohl, admitting the figures were the bleakest he had seen in his 14 years as chancellor, back-tracked on Friday by saying it was his goal, rather than his forecast, that unemployment be halved by 2000.
Opposition Social Democrat leaders were equally critical of Kohl, saying he had lost his authority and suggesting Germany's President Roman Herzog should help tackle the problems.

"Germany's president clearly has greater authority than the chancellor, especially after Kohl let last year's Alliance for Jobs to break down," Hans Eichel, premier of the state of Hesse, told newspaper Bild.

Last year, German employers, unions and government officials got together in an attempt to hash out new strategies to cut the jobless rate. But little progress was made, and unions now say Kohl failed to keep certain promises.

Kurt Beck, premier of the state of Rhineland-Palatinate, told Bild that immediate action needed to be taken on the jobs issue and that "it would be good sign if the president called key players in economics, politics and society to sit around one table."
To improve the situation, heads of Germany's trade union federation and the engineering employers federation Gesamtmetall pledged to join forces to try and reduce Germany's record high jobless rate.

Speaking together on German television late Friday, trade union federation DGB chief Dieter Schulte and Gesamtmetall head Werner Stumpfe demanded innovative steps to combat unemployment and suggested more part-time work could be useful.
Schulte said the amount of overtime hours worked must be reduced, adding that a further cut in the number of hours regularly worked could also help create new jobs.
